findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the cancelled request context
findings.body: Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection all launch `go func()` blocks that derive their timeout with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` from the incoming request context. The Kubernetes request context is cancelled as soon as the handler returns the storage result, which happens immediately after spawning the goroutine, so the legacy write will almost always run with an already-cancelled context and fail/abandon. A detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) before adding the timeout) is required, otherwise mode 3 silently does not perform the legacy writes it exists to perform as a safety net.

findings.title: Independent goroutines give no ordering for legacy writes
findings.body: Every write spawns an unsynchronised goroutine for the legacy store. A Create goroutine, a subsequent Update goroutine and a Delete goroutine for the same object can be scheduled or complete out of order (legacy latency is variable up to the 10s timeout): an update can run before the create it depends on and fail as not-found, or a delayed create can run after a delete and resurrect a deleted object in legacy storage. Mode 3 therefore can leave legacy permanently diverged from unified storage; legacy writes need to be serialised/queued per resource or otherwise ordered.

findings.title: Async legacy calls race on objects shared with the returned response
findings.body: Create passes the same `obj` pointer to Storage.Create and then to the background Legacy.Create while returning `created` to the caller, and Update passes the same `objInfo` (line 139) to both Storage.Update and the background Legacy.Update. The API server may serialise/mutate the returned object, and UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject may be invoked a second time against a different old object, concurrently with the first call and with response handling. This is a data race and can make the legacy copy differ from the object written to unified storage; the legacy goroutine needs its own deep copy / the precomputed updated object (as the previous updateWrapper approach provided).

findings.title: Storage failures are recorded as legacy metrics
findings.body: In Create, when d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) with the storage start time, and Update does the same at line 129. Storage failures are therefore attributed to the legacy duration metric (with the wrong latency) and no failing storage duration is recorded, corrupting the dual-writer dashboards/alerts used to judge migration safety. These should call recordStorageDuration. Conversely DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration for the legacy call, the mirror-image mistake.

findings.title: Delete records object name in the metric kind label
findings.body: On successful Delete the code calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage), passing the object `name` where every other call site passes options.Kind as the kind label. This creates one metric series per deleted object name (unbounded label cardinality in Prometheus) and makes per-kind aggregation impossible. It should pass options.Kind like the error path at line 103.

findings.title: Legacy write failures are never logged
findings.body: The background goroutines in Create, Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165) discard the legacy error except for a duration metric; the previous synchronous implementation logged these errors. Combined with the fire-and-forget design, an operator has no log signal (with kind/name) that legacy has diverged from unified storage and no way to know which objects need reconciliation. The error branch should log via the request-scoped logger before recording the metric.

findings.title: Mode 3 tests never verify the async legacy write happens
findings.body: The Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection tests register legacy mock expectations but return and assert on the storage result immediately, without waiting for the spawned goroutine or calling AssertExpectations/AssertCalled on the legacy mock (both mocks also share a single testify mock.Mock, so expectations cannot even distinguish the two stores). The tests pass even if the legacy write is removed entirely, and if the goroutine fires after the test finishes it can race with later tests using the shared mock and shared example objects. Tests need a synchronisation point (channel/WaitGroup in the mock or Eventually-style assertion) proving legacy is invoked with the right arguments.

findings.title: New mode 3 integration cases are flaky because legacy visibility is now asynchronous
findings.body: The added 'mode 3' subtests reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates/updates/deletes via the k8s API and then immediately asserts the objects are visible (and later gone) through the legacy /api/playlists endpoints. In mode 3 the legacy write is performed by a fire-and-forget goroutine started before the response returns, so there is no guarantee it has completed when the very next legacy request is made. These subtests will intermittently fail (missing/extra/stale playlists) unless the legacy assertions poll/wait for eventual consistency.
